proposal.summary: A logic bug in Linux kernel 6.2 can leave user processes vulnerable to cross-thread branch target injection (Spectre v2) when IBRS (but not enhanced IBRS) is used because the kernel disables STIBP and clears the IBRS bit on return to userspace, allowing other hyperthreads/processes on the same core to attack.
proposal.cwe_quote:
This happened because when plain IBRS was enabled (not enhanced IBRS), the kernel had some logic that determined that
[STIBP] was not needed. The IBRS bit implicitly protects against cross-thread
branch target injection. However, with legacy
[IBRS], the IBRS bit was cleared on returning to userspace, due to performance
reasons, which disabled the implicit STIBP and left userspace threads
vulnerable to cross-thread branch target injection against which STIBP
protects.

proposal.recommended_next_step: Confirm affected kernel trees and versions (verify presence of the cited code at arch/x86/kernel/cpu/bugs.c#L1196), reproduce on representative hardware (with and without SMT/eIBRS), and prepare a patch to ensure STIBP is enabled or IBRS bit is preserved for userspace when required.

evidence_quotes.claim: Vulnerability description (IBRS clears STIBP leaving userspace vulnerable)
evidence_quotes.quote:
This happened because when plain IBRS was enabled (not enhanced IBRS), the kernel had some logic that determined that
[STIBP] was not needed. The IBRS bit implicitly protects against cross-thread
branch target injection. However, with legacy
[IBRS], the IBRS bit was cleared on returning to userspace, due to performance
reasons, which disabled the implicit STIBP and left userspace threads
vulnerable to cross-thread branch target injection against which STIBP
protects.

The Bug present on Kernel 6.2
(https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v6.2/source/arch/x86/kernel/cpu/bugs.c#L1196)
implements an optimization that disables STIBP if the mitgation is
IBRS or eIBRS.

evidence_quotes.claim: Proof-of-concept shows attacker and victim processes on same core
evidence_quotes.quote:
The test consists of two processes. The attacker constantly poisons an
indirect call to speculatively redirect it to a target address. The
victim process measures the mispredict rate and tries to mitigate the
attack either by calling PRCTL or writing to the MSR directly using a
kernel module that exposes MSR read and write operations to userspace.
